1:
Fourteen years from what, and which journey? Ellicott finds ‘I went up again’ decisive for reckoning from the visit just mentioned, so the three years of the previous chapter must be added to reach the conversion, and identifies the journey with the Council of Jerusalem. Robertson agrees it is that conference, and notes another visit passed over in silence. Clarke reports a chronologer who counts instead from the conversion; Gill makes it seventeen; Luther eighteen. Wesley settles it in a clause: several passages here refer to that great council.

Calvin dissents outright. This cannot with certainty be affirmed the same journey the historian records; the connection of the history leads to the opposite conclusion. His argument is from the rebuke that follows: it is not reasonable that Peter would have used such dissimulation at Antioch if the decree of the apostles had already been published, so the rebuke, and therefore this visit, must fall earlier.

That he went up by revelation and yet was sent by a church looks like a discrepancy, and three remove it the same way. Barnes says there is none: though designated by the church at Antioch, he may also have been directed by a special revelation. Gill calls it a secret impulse of the Spirit, not inconsistent with being sent by the church, and confirming him that their decision was according to the mind of God. Ellicott states it most carefully: the inward guidance granted privately coincided with a formal commission from the church, and the external side of the transaction is naturally related by the historian while as naturally omitted by the apostle, whose thoughts are on his own motives. He adds that revelations came in several forms — dreams, nocturnal visions, a trance — and which was used here does not appear. Calvin presses the theological point: since God directed the journey, the doctrine was confirmed not by the concurrence of men only but by the authority of God, so the apostle was not made an apostle by them but acknowledged to be one.

Chrysostom alone stops at the difficulty in the reason given. What is this, he asks — thou who neither at the beginning nor after three years wouldest confer with the apostles, dost thou confer with them after fourteen, lest thou shouldest be running in vain? His answer is that the phrase about revelation, which seems to add a difficulty, in fact solves it: had the apostle gone up of his own accord it would have been folly, but going as the Spirit drew him there is no absurdity. Wesley reads the same words practically — lest he lose the fruit of present or past labours — and remarks that the word run beautifully expresses the swift progress of the gospel.

On the conference itself the details are shared out. Robertson names the three of repute and observes that their private decision would shape the public one, and that Titus, a Greek, appears nowhere in the history though his very presence was a challenge. Henry sets the scene: from the first planting of Christianity there was a difference between Christians who had first been Jews and those who had first been Gentiles, and the ceremonial law, dead with Christ, was not yet buried. Luther has the apostle offer the Jews a bargain — if that unprofitable service of the law so highly please you, keep it for me, so that the Gentiles be not charged with it — and insists the apostles taught him nothing. Tertullian turns the passage against an opponent who edited the text, observing how great the apostle’s desire was to be approved by the very men his adversary wished understood as allies of Judaism, and noting that the false brethren perverted the gospel not by expunging the Creator’s Christ from Scripture but by so retaining the old order as not to exclude the Creator’s law.
3:
Titus is the test case. Barnes calls it a case just in point: a man admitted to the church uncircumcised, brought to Jerusalem where the question was being decided, so settling his case settled the whole controversy about the Mosaic law and Gentile converts. Gill reads the silence as a measure of how complete the agreement was: Titus was on the spot, a Gentile, uncircumcised, and not even he was required. Clarke says the account was so satisfactory that the apostles did not even ask it, though at Jerusalem it might have looked expedient. Wesley draws the inference: clear proof that no apostle insisted on circumcising Gentile believers.

Then why circumcise Timothy? Four answer alike. Barnes: with Titus it was demanded as a matter of right and obligation, and he resisted the principle as dangerous; with Timothy it was voluntary compliance with a custom nobody pressed as indispensable, so no danger followed and it conciliated the Jews. Calvin puts it as a rule — if all things are lawful, ask what is expedient — and would gladly have circumcised Titus too, being unwearied in supporting the weak; but concealed foes who watch for our liberty must be vigorously resisted. Wesley compresses the distinction into a line: circumcising Timothy because of weak brethren, but not Titus because of false brethren. Ellicott alone concedes some real inconsistency here, though not more than anyone engaged in the struggles of active life is constantly drawn into; the meeting was a crisis where concession would have been fatal, while Timothy’s case was merely a practical compromise. He adds that Titus was wholly a Gentile, Timothy a Jew on his mother’s side.

Robertson refuses even the grammatical opening for a voluntary act: the verb is passive, and reading it to mean the apostle had Titus circumcised of his own accord is impossible in the light of the next verse and the context. On the intruders he notes a double compound found in the papyri in the sense of brought in on the sly, and a word for spying out that means to reconnoitre. Gill reports that Cerinthus was said to be at their head. Ellicott finds the sentence broken and imperfect, and would supply the missing clause — on account of false brethren I was urged to have him circumcised — making the leaders advise it as policy rather than require it.

Barnes proposes reading the third verse as a parenthesis, so that what the false brethren explain is not the refusal but the private interview, which was the way to counteract them. On the fifth verse he lays out the textual question. A considerable number of manuscripts omit the words to whom neither, reversing the sense into a brief yielding; that opinion has been gaining ground for a century, he says, but is by no means confirmed, since the ancient versions and by far the largest portion of manuscripts keep the usual reading. Ellicott, independently, finds the same omission in some early Latin authorities and calls it evidence of a very early corruption with no bearing on the exegesis.

Calvin makes the steadiness itself the seal of the doctrine: when men who wanted only a ground of accusation exerted themselves to the utmost and he stood firm, no room for doubt was left. He adds that there was no danger Paul would lose his liberty by yielding, but the example would have harmed others. Luther reads the outcome as a settled moderation: the Gentiles were not to be constrained, while circumcision was permitted the Jews for a time, not as necessary to righteousness but for reverence to the fathers and charity toward the weak. He denies flatly that circumcision was rejected as a damnable thing, and hears in the phrase the truth of the gospel its implied contrary — that there is a false gospel too, which does not deny faith but adds to it.
6:
Is ‘those who seemed to be somewhat’ a slight? Clarke says no: the verb is used by the best Greek writers not to call the sense in question but to deepen it, so it means those of acknowledged reputation. Calvin agrees, citing a lexical authority who finds the word used of the principal men of Greece. Gill guards it from the other side: nobody thought these men more than human, as Simon Magus gave out that he was some great one; nor were they something in name only, for they really were somewhat. Ellicott hears a certain amount of irony all the same, and insists on the present tense — not those who held authority at the Council, but those who are the great authorities with you Galatians now. Luther puts it hardest: he gives the true apostles no glorious title, as it were abasing their dignity, not to diminish their authority but because the false apostles were setting it against him everywhere.

Luther also supplies the argument being answered. They were conversant with Christ for three years and saw all his miracles, while Paul never saw him in the flesh and was converted long after; which then should you believe, one who was but a disciple and one of the last, or the chiefest apostles? The answer is that the controversy is not concerning the excellency of the apostles but the word of God.

On God accepting no man’s person, Ellicott gives the philology. To accept the face is used in the older Scriptures in the good sense of showing favour, without imputation of partiality; in the newer it always carries that idea, the word for face being used idiomatically for a mask, and so for a man’s outward and accidental characteristics as against his real character. Barnes draws the application: apostolic authority is not measured by external rank, or by reputation among men. Wesley says it in five words — for any eminence in gifts or outward prerogatives. Calvin defends the boasting against a charge of pride on practical grounds: had he conceded that he profited under the apostles, they would have said, so you corrected your past errors; his whole doctrine would have fallen under suspicion, and he would ever after have possessed less authority, reckoned but an ordinary disciple.

Then the division of spheres, and three voices raise the same objection independently. Barnes: it cannot mean that one preached only to Gentiles and the other only to Jews, for the apostle often preached in the synagogues and Peter was the first to preach to a Gentile; the point is each man’s main business. Luther presses the same counter-examples and answers historically — the others remained in Jerusalem until God called them elsewhere, and were dispersed only as the destruction of the city approached. Calvin sets it against the command to go into all the world, and replies that it was not meant to apply to each individual but describes in general the design of the apostolic office; then he adds, drily, that the apostles evidently did not travel over the whole world, that probably not one of the twelve ever passed into Europe, and that what they allege about Peter may be fabulous.

Ellicott ends on the translators: wrought effectually and was mighty are the same word in the Greek, and the doubling is an instance of a capriciousness due to their free poetic handling and superabundant command of words. Calvin is unsure whether the working means the success of the preaching or the graces then bestowed, and takes it as spiritual power and efficacy; either way the divine energy is the seal, so what the apostles settled between them was no idle bargain but a decision God had sealed. Robertson hears in it a complete answer to those who denied the apostleship because its holder was not one of the twelve.
9:
Clarke supplies the background to the word pillars, a small anthology. Among the Jews men of great eminence are represented as pillars of the world: Abraham is called the pillar of the universe, for by him to this day are the earth and heavens supported, and a dying teacher is addressed by his disciples as thou high pillar, thou light of the world, thou strong hammer. He then quotes the caution that goes with it: the pillars must be distinguished from the foundation, for the foundation of the Church is Christ alone, and the pillars are the more eminent teachers, which without the foundation are of no value. Ellicott confirms it, calling the metaphor natural, found in classical writers and in common use among the Jews for the great rabbinical teachers. Robertson keeps it concrete: an old word for columns, and these were the Pillar Apostles.

Why is James named first? Ellicott reports that a few manuscripts and patristic quotations read Peter, James and John, which doubtless arose from the tendency to exalt Peter, though the variant runs up into the second century and so is too early to be connected with the later pretensions of Rome. His own rule is that where the general work of the Church is in view Peter is prominent, and where a public act of the Church of Jerusalem is meant the precedence goes to James. Calvin finds the order surprising in a question of rank and offers the same solution, that James presided there. Wesley says simply, named first because he was bishop of the church in Jerusalem.

On the handshake the notes are complementary. Clarke gives the Hebrew idiom, in which deceiving a neighbour in what was delivered him to keep, or in fellowship, is literally deceiving him in the giving of the hand. Ellicott notes instances East and West where images of clasped hands were sent in suing for alliance. Robertson gives the moment: the concluding act of a pact for coordinate, independent spheres, where the compromisers and Judaizers were brushed aside as these five men shook hands as equals.

Why were the Judean brethren poor? Gill offers three causes and does not choose: the calamities of the nation, with a scarcity of provisions; the persecutions of their own countrymen, who plundered them of their goods for professing the name of Christ; or the exhaustion of the common stock into which they had at first given up all their substance. To the last he attaches an argument of equity — that fund had assisted the preachers who first carried the gospel to the Gentiles, so it was but just the Gentiles make some return. Calvin, who lists the first two causes and not the third, reaches the same equity by another road: it was proper they should receive assistance from the Gentiles, who owed them the inestimable benefit of the gospel. Barnes adds the domestic detail — a wife disowned by her husband, a child disinherited by a parent, a man thrown out of employment because others would not countenance him.

Barnes alone asks why the request needed making. It can hardly have needed stipulating for converts from among the Gentiles; the object was to bind the two bodies together, since it might have been alleged that the apostle was so entirely the apostle of the Gentiles that he had grown alienated from his kinsmen according to the flesh. Ellicott points out that the pledge was already a habit, contributions having been carried from Antioch before and gracefully received, not only as charity but as recognition of the claims of the mother Church. Luther generalises the clause into the pastoral office — where the church is there must needs be poor — then turns it against his own age, where a whole city thinketh much to find one or two poor ministers, which before sustained monasteries and whole swarms of priests.
11:
Was this Cephas the apostle at all? Gill reports the old dodge and dismisses it: several copies and old versions read Cephas, and some early writers held this to be one of the seventy bearing the same name — but without any manner of foundation, since the discourse shows the Cephas named just above with James and John is meant. Clarke says the controversy has lasted more than fifteen hundred years and is not yet settled, and that the reading hardly matters, since the question is the same either way; he notes drily that although some Catholic writers have fixed what is here reprehensible on a lesser Kephas, their own most learned writers and popes believe the apostle is meant.

Ellicott catalogues what the scene cost the early church. The Ebionites charged Paul with hostility to the faith for calling Peter condemned; Marcion saw proof of an antagonism between Judaism and Christianity; the critic Porphyry attacked both alike, one for error and the other for forwardness in rebuking it, and called the scene ecclesiastical wrangling. The unfortunate result was that orthodox writers set about explaining the plain narrative away — one Alexandrian holding that this Cephas was an inferior person, and a more popular theory, defended vehemently by Jerome, that the two had arranged the scene beforehand and acted it out for the edification of the Judaisers. That theory held its ground two centuries and was finally put down, Ellicott says, by the good sense of the bishop of Hippo.

Two voices reach the same polemical conclusion by opposite routes. Henry argues from the place: there is no colour of reason for supposing Peter was bishop of Antioch, for then Paul would not have withstood him in his own church; the rebuke is plain evidence that Paul was not inferior to him, and so of the weakness of the papal pretence to supremacy as his successor. Calvin argues from the manner: the reproof was not one Christian correcting another but an official act in the apostolic character — another thunderbolt striking the papacy, since a single individual chastises Peter before the whole Church, and Peter submissively bows.

On what Peter actually did, Robertson works from the tenses. He did eat with the Gentiles is an imperfect, so it was his habit; he drew back and separated himself are inchoative — he began to draw back, began to separate himself, just like a Pharisee. The real reason was not a change of view but pure fear of trouble to himself, as in the denials at the trial. On the men from James, Robertson doubts they were sent: they let the idea get out that they were his emissaries, but that is inconsistent with his position as author of the resolution securing Gentile liberty; more likely they threatened to tell him. Barnes states flatly that James had nothing to do with their course.

Luther insists on the exact charge: Paul accuses him not of malice or ignorance but of dissimulation and infirmity, reproving not the transgression but the dissembling, since in eating with the Gentiles Peter had done well and knew it. What the withdrawal did was plant a syllogism in weak consciences: Peter abstained from meats forbidden in the law, therefore he that eats them sins. Then the loneliness of it: Paul alone standeth to the truth, for he had lost Barnabas his companion, and Peter was against him; so sometimes one man is able to do more in a council than the whole council besides. Barnabas is what the others fasten on. Clarke calls him the gentle, loving-hearted Barnabas, carried away by their hypocrisy; Wesley says he was borne away as with a torrent; Robertson calls it a solemn moment when Paul saw the Jerusalem victory vanish and Barnabas desert him; Ellicott suggests the breach which soon led to the definite separation of the two apostles is traceable here.
14:
The verb is rare and everyone stops on it. Ellicott notes that walked not uprightly is one Greek word, found here alone in the New Testament, meaning literally to walk on straight feet, as against shuffling; Robertson adds that it turns up afterwards only in ecclesiastical writers. Gill hears the prophets in it: they halted, as the Jews of old, between two opinions, partly for God and partly for Baal, and made not straight paths for their feet but crooked ones.

On why the rebuke was public, Barnes is fullest. Had this been private he would have sought a private interview; but it was public, many were involved, and fixed principles had to be settled. He draws three inferences: that the reprover was regarded as Peter’s equal; that public reproof is right when the offence has been public; and that reproving those who err is a duty, painful and neglected. Calvin reaches the same rule: those who have sinned publicly must be publicly chastised, lest the sin form a dangerous example; and the direction that elders be rebuked before all applies here because their station renders their example more pernicious. Wesley puts the scene in a phrase: see Paul single against Peter and all the Jews. Robertson allows himself an aside: one is a bit curious what those who consider Peter the first pope will do with this open rebuke.

Clarke feels the sting of the question. It was a cutting reproof, for here was a man scrupulous in everything relative to the law, whom it took a miracle to convince that the Gentiles were admitted on believing. Thou didst once consider they were not under such an obligation, and now actest as if the law were in full force; thou art convinced of the contrary, yet actest differently. This, says Clarke, is hypocrisy. Ellicott sharpens the wording: being a Jew is emphatic, with all the antecedents of a Jew, which implies a different rule for men of wholly different antecedents; compellest means do what you can to compel. Robertson calls it a bold thrust that allowed no reply, and notes that Paul won Peter back, and Barnabas also.

Calvin is careful about what was not at stake. On doctrine the two were perfectly agreed, and he quotes an authority that neither apostle had fallen into error in faith, the controversy relating not to the doctrine of Christian liberty but to the exercise of it at different times and places, on which point the rules of prudence were better understood by Paul than by Peter. But laying doctrine out of view, Peter yielded too submissively, and so is accused of halting. Calvin refuses the excuse others offer, that as apostle of the circumcision Peter owed a particular concern to the Jews: it is foolish to defend what the Holy Spirit by the mouth of Paul has condemned.

Luther fastens on the blindness. None but Paul hath his eyes open and seeth the offence; the others do not see their own, but think they do well in bearing with the infirmities of the weak. It is a great matter that Peter should be accused of falling from the truth of the Gospel — he could not be more grievously reprehended — yet he suffered it patiently. Many have the Gospel but not the truth of the Gospel: these preached it, yet through a dissimulation which could not stand with it they established the law, and the establishing of the law is the abolishing of the Gospel. His remedy is to keep the two apart by force: place the Gospel in heaven and the law on earth, and put as great difference between their righteousnesses as God hath between light and darkness. Then the admission that gives the rule its weight — in the time of temptation, I confess that I myself do not know how to do it as I ought.
15:
Who is addressed from here on? Barnes lays it out: some hold the narrative closes and the argument turns to the Galatians, others that the address to Peter runs to the chapter’s end. He takes the second — it is the most natural reading, the real change of address comes at the next chapter, and the objection that it is incongruous to lecture Peter on justification fails, since the reproof was before them all and served everyone in danger of the error. Robertson leaves it open: the writer may be mentally addressing Peter, if not quoting him. Wesley notices the pronoun: to spare Peter he drops the singular and speaks in the plural.

On Jews by nature, Clarke goes to the stones. The word signifies not by nature as we use the phrase, but the birth, family or nation of a man; and he cites a Greek marble where a man says of his son-in-law that he is called a Jasian and of the house of Milesius, though by nature from Jaso. Gill sorts the senses: Jews by grace, Jews by proselytism, and these, Jews by birth, bred from infancy under the law. Ellicott hears irony in the second half — sinners was almost a synonym for heathen in a strict Jew’s mouth, so the concession runs: from our lofty position we can look down on those poor Gentiles, sinners by mere descent.

Calvin treats the verse as an anticipated objection turned round. The Jews, holy so far as God had chosen them, might contend for the superiority — and that is what condemns them. If the law were advantageous for salvation to those who observed it, it must have been most advantageous to us to whom it was given; but if we relinquished it for Christ, much less ought compliance be urged on the Gentiles. Luther presses the premise harder before breaking it: we are born righteous, our righteousness beginneth with our birth, for the Jewish religion is natural unto us — and yet we are not therefore righteous before God.

Ellicott and Calvin converge on the little word that follows. Ellicott renders it except, referring only to justified and not to the preceding denial of works: a man is not justified by works, nor justified at all, except by faith in Christ. Calvin insists on the same exclusiveness for polemical reasons. The false apostles rejected neither Christ nor faith, but demanded that ceremonies be joined with them; had Paul allowed that, they would have been perfectly at one, and he need not have agitated the church with this debate. Hence, he adds, it appears with what silly trifling the Papists dispute about the word alone, as if it were a word of our contrivance — for of such half-justification, making part of justification consist in works, Paul knew nothing.

How far do the works of the law reach? Wesley says not even of the moral, much less the ceremonial, and notes that the argument has quietly widened: hitherto the question was the ceremonial law, but by citing the psalm the apostle insensibly goes farther. Luther makes the rule absolute — whatsoever is not grace is law, judicial, ceremonial, or the ten commandments — and then reaches for pagan examples: Cicero suffered death valiantly in a good cause, and another Roman loved truth so well he never made a lie nor suffered one in another — noble virtues and excellent works of the law, yet these men were not justified thereby. Ellicott notes that the closing quotation has no exact equivalent in the older Scriptures, the nearest being the psalm saying that in thy sight shall no man living be justified. Barnes gives the verse the title Luther gave the doctrine, the article of a standing or falling church; and Henry adds that the charge that justification by faith alone encourages sin is no new prejudice, though most unjust.
17:
Barnes admits the connexion here is not very clear and the sense somewhat obscure. Barnes prefers the objection brought in every age — that justification by faith leads to licentiousness, since it does not require obedience, pronounces a man justified who violates the law, and makes acceptance independent of moral character. He puts the challenge in the objector’s voice: if your lives turn out not to be holy, does it not follow that Christ taught it, and that the system he introduced is responsible?

Calvin and Barnes then part company over something basic — whether Peter is still being addressed. Calvin says we must not connect this verse with the speech to Peter — what had Peter to do with this argument? Barnes holds the address runs to the end of the chapter, noting that one commentator puts the break at the next verse.

What made these men sinners? Calvin’s answer is the sharpest. While still at a distance from Christ, Jews appear in some respects exempted from the appellation of sinner; the grace of Christ places them on a level with the Gentiles, and the remedy, common to both, shews that both had laboured under the same disease. Robertson says the same biographically: Jews who thought they were not sinners, brought close to Christ, found that they were; to call him a minister of sin on that account is an illogical inference — Christ simply revealed to us our sin. Ellicott splits the word in two: sinners actually, through positive transgressions, and sinners judicially, since on the Judaising theory the old justification through fulfilment of the Law has been given up while the new is declared insufficient.

Ellicott then turns it into a trap for the Judaisers. You call yourselves Christians, he has the apostle say, and yet insist upon the Mosaic law; you say a man cannot be justified without it; it follows that we, who exchanged the Law for Christ, are not justified — our relation to Christ has made us not better but worse, a thought no Christian can entertain. The sin, he adds, is seen doubly: on the theory that the Law is valid it was wrong to give it up, and on the theory that Christianity has taken its place it is worse still to restore the fabric once broken down. Luther reduces it to an either-or: one of the two must be false, either we are not justified by Christ or not by the law; and since we are justified by Christ, we are not justified by the law. Clarke locates the self-contradiction one step back: by submitting to circumcision we lay ourselves under the necessity of fulfilling a law impossible to fulfil, and so constitute ourselves sinners.

On the rebuilding, Ellicott notices the courtesy in the grammar: the first person is used out of delicate consideration for the opponents; the apostle puts a supposed case which really represents what they were doing, and takes it on himself to soften the reference. He notes how fond this writer is of metaphors of building and pulling down, and sums the verse in a proverb: burn what you have adored, and adore what you have burned. Robertson makes it merciless: Peter by his shifts had contradicted himself helplessly, for when he lived like a Gentile he tore down the ceremonial law, and when he lived like a Jew he tore down salvation by grace. Luther supplies the image: when the new guest, Christ Jesus, cometh into the new house, there to dwell alone, Moses the old inhabiter must give place unto him and depart some whither else. Gill adds a distinction: the things destroyed are not the good things he once destroyed and now builds, but the rites now abrogated. Wesley closes the objection off — it were just, if the gospel promised justification to men continuing in sin, but it does not.
19:
Through which law? Barnes says commentators are by no means agreed. Some take it of the Christian religion — by one law or doctrine I am dead to another; most take it of the law of Moses, so that by contemplating its character, design and requisitions he had become dead to it. Barnes prefers the second, and makes it autobiographical: he had expected to be justified by the law and endeavoured to obey it, but when he was made to feel its spiritual requirements, all his hopes of justification by it died. Clarke will not choose, offering both readings in a breath; Gill takes the first, noting that the Hebrew word answering to law signifies properly doctrine, sometimes the doctrine of the gospel.

What is being dead to it? Barnes offers the plain figure: a dead man is insensible to all around him; he hears nothing, sees nothing, nothing affects him. Gill fences the figure with the most careful qualifications in the chapter: dead to the law not so as to disregard it as a rule of walk and conversation, but so as not to seek life and righteousness by it, nor to fear its accusations, menaces and curses; dead to the moral law in the hands of Moses, but not in the hands of Christ; dead to it as a covenant of works, though not as a rule of action.

Ellicott notices that the pronoun has changed owners. The I of the previous verse is really Peter or the Judaisers; the I of this one is the apostle himself. His reading of the paradox: the road to freedom from the Law lay through the Law. On its prophetic side the Law pointed to Christ; on its moral side it held up an ideal its votaries could not attain and it did not help them attain, so bearing the stamp of its own insufficiency. Hence his striking claim: Paul would not have become a Christian if he had not first sat at the feet of Gamaliel.

Calvin makes the verse the direct reply: the work must not be laid at the wrong door, for it was not necessary that Christ should destroy the righteousness of the law — the law itself slays its disciples. He puts it to the opponents as a speech: you deceive wretched men by the false notion that they must live by the law, and yet you charge the Gospel with annihilating the righteousness we have by the law; but it is the law which forces us to die to itself. He also wants the sentence repointed: the ordinary punctuation obscures the meaning, and the clause about living to God reads better joined forward — that I might live to God, I am crucified with Christ.

Luther calls these marvellous words, unknown kinds of speech which man’s reason can in no wise understand. His account is that grace itself is here called the law, a new name for the working of grace, in contempt of the law of Moses, so that law is set against law — a sweet kind of speech, of the same family as sin against sin, death against death, the lamb against the lamb. This law accuseth the accusing law, and condemneth the condemning law. Then he presses it to scandal: here Paul seemeth to be a heretic, yea, of all heretics the greatest, for the false apostles taught that except thou live to the law thou art dead to God, and he saith quite contrary, that except thou be dead to the law thou canst not live to God. Robertson dispatches the paradox in three words: paradoxical, but true. Wesley supplies the missing agent: the law was applied by the Spirit to his heart, deeply convincing him of his utter sinfulness and helplessness; and for this very end is he freed from the law, that he may be freed from sin.
20:
Two voices reach the same lexical fact from opposite ends. Gill says the crucifixion is not literal, for so only the two thieves were crucified with him, but mystical: Christ was crucified in his room and stead, so their old man was crucified with him when the body of their sins was laid on him. Robertson, calling this one of Paul’s greatest mystical sayings, notes that the compound verb occurs in the Gospels of the robbers’ literal crucifixion. Barnes works the figure out: the Redeemer on the cross became insensible to all surrounding objects, as the dead always are, and so this man became dead to the law, to the world, to ambition and the love of money, to the pomp of life. The union he illustrates twice: a blow at the root of a vine affects every branch, a blow at the head every member.

Ellicott and Robertson part company over how hard to press it. Robertson says the identification is so complete that the separate personality is merged in Christ. Ellicott will not go there: the idea of union with Christ, pressed to precise logical definition, must contain a certain element of metaphor, and consciousness, rigorously examined, tells us that even in the most exalted souls there is no actual union of the human and divine. What he grants is still large — an influence from above so penetrating and powerful that the figure of union could alone express it.

Calvin gives the life a botanical shape, then divides it. Ingrafted into the death of Christ we derive from it a secret energy, as the twig does from the root. Christ lives in us, he says, in two ways: the one in governing us by his Spirit and directing all our actions, the other in making us partakers of his righteousness, so that while we can do nothing of ourselves we are accepted before God — the first relating to regeneration, the second to justification by free grace. On the life now lived in the flesh he reports that hardly a sentence here has not been torn by a variety of interpretations. Some understand the word of the depravity of sinful nature; he takes it as the bodily life, and answers the paradox by saying that the life consists in faith, a secret hidden from the senses of man, not visible to the bodily eye but inwardly perceived in the conscience.

Luther takes up the correction in the sentence itself. He notes the direction of the language — he saith we are dead and crucified to the law, whereas in very deed the law itself is dead and crucified unto us, and this of purpose, that it may be the more sweet and comfortable. Then the pronoun: who is that I, of whom he saith, yet not I? This I is he which hath the law and is bound to do the works thereof, a person separate from Christ, whom he rejecteth. Then the image, with an apology for its coarseness: he is my form, my furniture and perfection, adorning my faith as the colour, the clear light, or the whiteness do garnish and beautify the wall — thus are we constrained grossly to set forth this matter, for we cannot spiritually conceive Christ so nearly joined unto us.

The last clause draws the shortest sayings. Clarke has it in six words: Christ is the soul of my soul. Wesley calls him a fountain of life in the inmost soul, from which all my tempers, words and actions flow. Henry turns it into a test: to believe in Christ crucified is not only to believe that he was crucified, but that I am crucified with him. And on the singular pronoun Robertson quotes a commentator: he appropriates to himself the love which belongs equally to the whole world, for Christ is the personal friend of each man individually.
21:
The verb first. Barnes says it means properly to displace, abrogate, abolish, then to make void; Robertson calls it a common word in the Greek version and the historians, meaning to make ineffective. Gill runs through the old versions — cast it away, deny it, despise, reject, make it void. Ellicott turns the sense into an image: the grace of God goes forth with a mission to perform, and the Judaising party, by clinging to the Law, prevented it from taking effect and made it return void unto its Giver.

Then the force of in vain, where Calvin makes a correction. He cites an authority that the word means not in vain, uselessly or ineffectually, but without just cause: if righteousness be by the law, there was no reason why he should die. Robertson reaches it by grammar, an adverbial accusative of the word for a gift — Christ died gratuitously, unnecessarily. Wesley says it plainly: without any necessity for it, since men might have been saved without his death, and by their own obedience both discharged from condemnation and entitled to life.

Calvin then argues backwards from the names given that death, in the tightest sentence in the chapter: if the death of Christ be our redemption, we were captives; if it be satisfaction, we were debtors; if it be atonement, we were guilty; if it be cleansing, we were unclean. He also refuses the compromise before it is offered. We shall be told that the argument has no weight against those who unite the grace of Christ with works, since the two doctrines stand together, righteousness being partly by the law and partly from grace; but such theology, he says, was unknown to Paul, whose argument is either conclusive or inconclusive. And where others confine the verse to the ceremonial law, he asks who does not see that it applies to the whole.

Barnes draws the practical consequence as a question. If a man could be justified by conformity to any law, the work would have been wholly in his own power and the merit his own, and no atonement was needed; which is why those who depend on their own morality feel no need of a Saviour — for why should a man in health employ a physician? Robertson presses the point outward: this verse is a complete answer to those who say the heathen, or any mere moralist, are saved by doing the best they know and can, since no one apart from Jesus ever did the best he knew or could. Ellicott adds why the Law could never do it: it professed to make righteous those who complied with its provisions, but that was only a profession, for no one could really keep it.

Clarke closes with a reflection on the chapter as a whole: an argument from embarrassment. Worldly prudence and fleshly wisdom would have concealed this account of the prevarication of Peter, but God tells truth: if the Gospel were not of God we had never heard of it, nor of the contention between Paul and Barnabas. Had the apostles acted in concert to impose a forgery on the world as a divine revelation, the imposture would have come out, for the falling out of the parties would have led to a discovery of the cheat; so this relation is an additional evidence of the truth of the Gospel. He adds that no person in a state of probation is infallible, and that these accounts are recorded not that men may excuse their own delinquencies, but that they may avoid them. Luther ends on the strangeness of the charge: who hath ever heard that a man, by keeping of the law, rejecteth grace? Do we then sin in keeping the law? No, forsooth — but we despise grace when we observe the law to this end, that we may be justified through it.
